واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

The Grapes of Wrath is, the narrator tells us, a book, Pilgrim's Progress . "My father had it. He liked a book," muses one of the women. "Used to read it" (GW 120). Though The Grapes of Wrath describes the journey of an oppressed people to a Promised Land largely through allusions to Old Testament biblical material, chiefly from the Book of Exodus, but with rich additions taken from other biblical stories (see, among others, Shockley, Lisca, Crockett, Fontenrose, Hunter, Rombold, Perkin), it also does so through a concerted, grim modernization of Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress , a work that, as Steinbeck stated in his introduction to The Acts of King Arthur and his Noble Knights , was "mixed with [his] mother's milk" (xi). Stephen Railton has argued that The Grapes of Wrath is, like The Pil- grim's Progress , about conversion, that Route 66 "runs parallel to the road to Damascus that Saul takes in Acts, or to the Way taken by Bunyan's Christian in The Pilgrim's Progress " (29). The most meaningful events of the novel, he suggests, are the conversions of Casy and Tom, and later of Rose of Sharon. In Railton's view, in his attention to such transformations, Steinbeck emphasizes the necessity both of socio-political change and of psycho-spiritual readiness to embrace and enact it. Railton's reading of The Grapes of Wrath as a contemporized Pilgrím's Progress deserves further attention. The parallels between the two books are striking, and the variations that Steinbeck performs upon Bunyan's spiritual tract suggest his indebtedness to this great work of Christian faith as well as his fundamental disagreement with its tenets. The multiplicity of passages that specifically evoke The Pilgrim's Progress has not yet been fully recognized, in part, perhaps, because of the proliferation of commentary on Steinbeck's biblical allusions, which dominated critical attention to the novel in the 1950s and 1960s, and in part because The Pilgrim's Progress itself is saturated with the imagery and tone of many of the scriptural stories that are invoked in Stein- beck's fiction. The comingling of the two works adds richness and density - and heightened irony - to Steinbeck's epic narration of human pilgrimage. Steinbeck, in effect, in addition to recasting the Book of Exodus and the Passion © 2010 The Martha Heasley Cox Center for Steinbeck Studies/Wiley Periodicals, Inc. ELIZABETH NAPIER and Resurrection of Christ, also structures The Grapes of Wrath explicitly as a revised Pilgrim's Progress , one in which the Celestial City is exposed as a sham, divine guidance is absent, and there is active discouragement of the type of exegesis that gives Bunyan's work its weight and meaning. Like The Pilgrim's Progress , The Grapes of Wrath is a journey, a quest for salvation, a flight from uthe wrath to come " (PP 41). The trope lends cohesion to the various incidents in which the endurance and faith of both Bunyan's and Steinbeck's pilgrims are tested, compelling, as Railton has noted, action on their parts and dramatizing the oppressive pressure that environment and circumstance exert upon them (32). But the differences between the two paths or ways are striking. Bunyan's Christian begins his journey by leaving his family, though his wife and children "cry after him to return" (PP 41): for Bunyan, the quest for salvation is a radically individual one, entail- ing both a conviction of sin and a rejection of community (indeed, of the secu- lar world altogether). Steinbeck, however, early in The Grapes of Wrath makes short work of the doctrine of original sin in Casy's repudiation of the con- ventional definition of unrighteousness (GW 31-33), and sin eventually comes to be identified as a socio-political evil, outside the self and anterior to any A bas-reliet trom Pilgrim s Progress (167ö; on the base ot the statue ot John Bunyan in Bedford, sculpted by Joseph Edgar Boehm. THE GRAPES OF WRATH theological realm: "bein' hungry ... bein' cold" (GW 423). In Steinbeck's emphatically social world, his Joads, unlike their virtually solitary counter- part, Christian, ply their way as a family, with the interpretation of that unit becoming not less but more expansive as the novel proceeds, from the welcoming of Jim Casy into the group, to the adoption of the Wilsons, to the magnificent scene with which the novel closes. Indeed, the need to transform the Bunyanesque "I" into a socialized "we" (a "we" that far transcends blood ties) forms the subject of Steinbeck's important Chapter Fourteen. And as he does with the turns he executes on the Book of Exodus, so he creates likenesses to and performs revisions on Bunyan's ideas of heavenly bliss and of the faith and the guidance that such visions require. On his way, Bunyan's Christian is fortified by a vision of a Kingdom of Heaven in which "there shall be no more crying, nor sorrow There we shall be with seraphims, and chérubins" (PP 44). His rapturous descriptions to Pliable (44) and those that conclude the first part of The Pilgrim's Progress (200-04) are echoed in the Oklahoma families' vision of California as "nice Never cold . . . fruit ever'place, an' . . . little white houses in among the orange trees" - "grapes out there, just a-hangin' over inta the road," as Grampa puts it (GW 124, 126). Though the kingdom that the Joads seek is, in keeping with Steinbeck's focus on the secular and the socio-economic, comparatively humble, the prospect of stability and plenty (the promise of the orange handbills, to which the men refer in times of trouble) sustains them in their passage. But the handbills, unlike Christian's certificate of election, offer false comfort, and the actively doubting Jim Casy (nominally the religious "leader" of the pilgrimage) purveys not the awful, ultimate Truth of Bunyan's Evangelist (on which Christian unequivocally relies) but skepticism about conventional religious faith and practices, a non- Bunyanesque conviction that for strength and direction one must rely solely on oneself. The central importance of the truck in the novel (its torturous progress, Steinbeck's attention to its inner workings and breakdowns) epitomizes Stein- beck's fierce secularization of Bunyan's allegory. Although Steinbeck leads the Joads forth in a fashion that recalls the linear progress of The Pilgrim's Progress and into places that occasionally echo points along Christian's Way, the topography of Steinbeck's novel is recognizably real, unlike the symbolic landscape through which Christian moves (though perhaps no less grotesque). Strikingly Bunyan-like is Steinbeck's tendency in charting the Joads' progress to focus on specific, often bizarre characters or settings from whom or from which wisdom (of some kind or another, usually negative) may be gleaned. Thus, the work moves forward in the first section largely through Bunyanesque vignettes: the exchanges in Chapters Six and Ten with Muley, who, like Obstinate and Steinbeck Review 53 All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

ELIZABETH NAPIER Pliable, stays behind; the meeting with the man at the gasoline station in Chapter Thirteen; the encounter in Chapter Sixteen with the one-eyed man, who resembles, as he delivers his mantras of despair, Bunyan's Man in the Iron Cage (PP 65-67); the scene at the diner in Chapter Fifteen, which echoes and then negates Bunyan's House Beautiful, in which the family barters for ten cents worth of bread and the damsel Mae initially withholds food and relief; the later sojourn at Weedpatch, which resembles Christian's respite in the Delectable Mountains; and, most Bunyanesque of all, the ragged man in the camp ground of Chapter Sixteen, whose demoniac laughter vividly recalls that of Bunyan's Atheist, who, returning from his quest "with his back toward Sion . . . , [falls] into a very great laughter," intimating the darkest possibility of all: that "there is no such place as you dream of in all this world" (PP 174): "I'm comin' back," the ragged man intones. "I been there" (GW 257). Indeed, at this juncture, the "terrible faith" (GW 165) of the migrant families is sorely tried: they move on from here in full, but perhaps unconscious, recognition that there is no Mount Sion, no heavenly Jerusalem. Steinbeck's is a world in which Demas is in charge, a universe in which an outward event (a punctured tire, a burning camp) conceals no mystic meaning (as in The Pilgrim's Progress ), but which demands scrutiny and solution on its own terms, a place in which fatigue is not an indication of spiritual backsliding but a physical symptom of earthly things gone hideously awry. As the Joad men, prior to the crossing of the desert, bathe in the river en route to Needles in Chapter Eighteen, not only is Bunyan's symbolically charged geography pointedly inverted; but also no holy transformation occurs. Indeed, Pa and his sons are joined by men who are "goin' back" (GW 278), who revive the men's doubts about the California promise, forecasting a place of suspicion, racial hatred, and fear that will nourish a loss of faith ("You gonna think all the scales is crooked, an' you don' know which ones" [GW 281]). This episode of spiritual cleansing ("Jesus," exclaims Tom, as they enter the great valley and as he takes account of the fiscal and emotional toll of their journey, "are we gonna start clean! We sure ain't bringin' nothin' with us" [314]) is followed not by passage to Mount Sion (as in Bunyan's work) but by Noah's defection. And, in a cruel reversal of the sequence of The Pil- grim's Progress , the crossing of the desert, Steinbeck's Valley of the Shadow of Death ("dangerous" [GW 301], "terrible" [GW 302], "bones ever'place" [GW 276]), results not (as in The Pilgrim's Progress ) in deliverance but in Granma's demise and the yet more harrowing trials and humiliations that await them in California. The subsequent course of Steinbeck's novel opens the narrative to a place that the reader glimpses only for an ecstatic moment in The Pilgrim's Progress 54 Steinbeck Review All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

THE GRAPES OF WRATH before Bunyan's dreamer awakens and the first part of the allegory ends. Steinbeck, in contrast, forcibly enters the Gates with his pilgrims, conducting, over the course of the novel's furious second half, an excoriating exposé of the Celestial City, with shining angels and the Heavenly King replaced by vigilante mobs and corrupt overseers, and with the confirmation of faith sealed by a stirring of revolution and violent union, a fomenting of anger (GW 388) that is the antithesis to Bunyan's melodious choir of angels bearing harps and crowns and welcoming Christian into their midst with loud rejoicing (PP 202-03). The scenes of Casy's death, Tom's exile, the flood, and the birth and launching forth of Rose of Sharon's dead child on the flood waters all reveal Steinbeck's fevered grappling with the enduring economic and spiritual horrors of the Promised Land. Steinbeck's invocation of The Pilgrim's Progress , interwoven as it is and often conjoined with the rich texture of biblical allusions that distinguishes Steinbeck's greatest work, is thus echoed more frequently and more specifically than has been heretofore recognized. Not only does he systematically, in the sequential structure of the first section of his novel, recall to mind a fundamen- tal work on Christian faith and endurance, he uses The Pilgrim's Progress as a source from which to craft a view of salvation that is communal, fierce, icon- oclastic, political - one that shares the intensity of Bunyan's Puritan tract but that is radically different from that of his authorial and ideological predecessor in its rejection of the idea of original sin and in its embrace of a collective that must find the force to guide itself in a world of horrific inequities and corruption.
